MicroBiotR: runnable tutorial

MicroBiotR developers

1 Introduction

This notebook contains all 15 analysis steps from the repository README. The workflows are independent: cytometry runs steps 1–13, 16s runs step 14, and rna runs step 15. Choose all to run all three.

The default is the smaller 16S example. Choose your workflow in the YAML parameters before execution.

Results are exploratory. Feature selection and evaluation on the same samples do not establish independent predictive performance. Full cytometry training uses the large example dataset and can take substantial time and memory.

  1. Install MicroBiotR and its dependencies using the repository README. Install rmarkdown, knitr, and tidyverse as well. Cytometry density plots also require hexbin. RStudio supplies Pandoc for HTML rendering.
  2. Save this .Rmd in a new analysis folder and open it in RStudio.
  3. Set workflow, data_dir, and output_dir in the YAML header above. Relative paths resolve from the notebook’s folder when knitting.
  4. Put the matching files from Zenodo in data_dir, or set download_data: true to download missing files. The cytometry dataset is approximately 539 MB and training is expensive.
  5. Select Run All to execute chunks interactively. Preview shows a notebook with saved chunk outputs. To execute the entire document and create a standalone HTML report, use Knit to HTML or:
rmarkdown::render("MicroBiotR-tutorial.Rmd", output_format = "html_document")

Override the YAML parameters when rendering, for example:

rmarkdown::render("MicroBiotR-tutorial.Rmd", output_format = "html_document",
                  params = list(workflow = "rna", data_dir = "data",
                                output_dir = "results"))

Set execute: false to render the explanatory text and code without running analyses or downloading data. Set reuse_som: true for cytometry only when results/cytometry/SOM.csv, cluster_information.csv, and MappedFCS/ already contain outputs from step 1 for the same input data. Output filenames are reused on subsequent runs; use a new output_dir to keep runs separate. No packages are installed or upgraded by this notebook.

2 Environment Setup

3 Configuration

data.frame(workflow = params$workflow,
           reused_som = run_flow && isTRUE(params$reuse_som),
           MicroBiotR = as.character(packageVersion("MicroBiotR")))

4 Input Data

Workflow Data Metadata
Cytometry data_gated.save meta.txt
16S bac_data.txt bac_meta.txt
RNA rnaibd.csv meta_rna.txt

Files are checked against the record’s published MD5 checksums before use. Existing files are never automatically replaced if their checksums differ.

expected_md5 <- c(
  "meta_rna.txt" = "857b837d31314ce1e82a99c901c948b8",
  "data_gated.save" = "7045a1ed0405737eae874acd58d74f0d",
  "meta.txt" = "86e78fdd5d1661e1d01ad9029bfa8509",
  "bac_meta.txt" = "9acedac7d5c1bcd312dce6094779ea60",
  "bac_data.txt" = "6d3660887072b4f6c70d5bd7b445567a",
  "rnaibd.csv" = "c14e65cdbcbe84cd1e5bea49af2ee615"
)
required_files <- c(
  if (run_flow) c("data_gated.save", "meta.txt"),
  if (run_16s) c("bac_data.txt", "bac_meta.txt"),
  if (run_rna) c("rnaibd.csv", "meta_rna.txt")
)
for (name in required_files) {
  path <- file.path(data_dir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    if (!isTRUE(params$download_data)) {
      stop("Missing example file: ", path, ". Download it from Zenodo or set download_data: true.")
    }
    previous_timeout <- getOption("timeout")
    options(timeout = max(1800, previous_timeout))
    tryCatch({
      url <- paste0("https://zenodo.org/records/20286378/files/", name, "?download=1")
      utils::download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", method = "libcurl")
    }, finally = options(timeout = previous_timeout))
  }
  if (!identical(unname(tools::md5sum(path)), unname(expected_md5[name]))) {
    stop("Checksum mismatch for ", path, ". Replace the incomplete or changed file with the Zenodo example.")
  }
}
data.frame(file = required_files, verified = TRUE)

5 Cytometry workflow (steps 1–13)

These chunks run when workflow is cytometry or all. Study-specific cluster IDs and channel labels below refer to the supplied BD Influx example. Confirm sample IDs and channel scales when adapting them to another experiment.

5.1 Step 1: SOM analysis

A self-organizing map (SOM) represents similar flow events with shared multichannel prototypes. Mapping each sample to the same prototypes creates comparable cluster abundance profiles. Channel scales influence the fit, and training can require substantial time and memory.

meta <- read.delim(file.path(data_dir, "meta.txt"), header = TRUE, row.names = 1)
set.seed(2025)
if (isTRUE(params$reuse_som)) {
  count_table <- read.csv(file.path(flow_out, "SOM.csv"), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
  cohonen_information <- read.csv(file.path(flow_out, "cluster_information.csv"),
                                   row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
  if (!dir.exists(file.path(flow_out, "MappedFCS"))) stop("reuse_som requires the mapped FCS directory.")
} else {
  load(file.path(data_dir, "data_gated.save"))
  MBR_som(fl_data_ig, out_path = flow_out)
}
# Check sample identity before downstream tests; ordering is handled by MicroBiotR.
stopifnot(setequal(rownames(count_table), rownames(meta)),
          ncol(count_table) == 2025L, all(abs(rowSums(count_table) - 1) < 1e-8))

5.2 Step 2: Statistics

Compare feature abundances between groups using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test. False discovery rate (FDR) adjustment accounts for testing many features. Interpret associations at the biological sample level and consider the compositional nature of relative abundances.

# Test options are 'wilcox', 'kruskal', 'anova', 't.test' or 'ttest'.
# correction could be one of 'none', 'fdr', 'bonferroni' ,'BH'
MBR_stat(data = count_table, group_col = 'Group', meta_data = meta,
       # Use the two-sided Wilcoxon group test.
       test_type = 'wilcox', out_path = flow_out,
       # Set whether feature-wise p-values are adjusted for multiple tests.
       correction = 'fdr', cutoff = 0.001)

5.3 Step 3: Circular heatmap

A circular heatmap summarizes average abundance in each group. The difference track helps identify clusters with contrasting group means; it is a descriptive display rather than an additional hypothesis test.

# Generate a circular plot to visualize significant features across groups
MBR_circle(
  # dataframe containing features
  data = significant_data,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_col = 'Group',
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta,
  # width of the output figure
  width = 16,
  # height of the output figure
  height = 16,
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out
)

5.4 Step 4: Cluster abundance violin plot

Inspect how one cluster is distributed across samples in each group. The violin shows distribution shape, the box plot summarizes the median and interquartile range, and the annotation displays the previously calculated adjusted p-value.

# Generate a violin plot for a selected feature/cluster
MBR_violin(
  # dataframe containing features
  data = significant_data,
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_col = "Group",
  # statistical test result dataframe containing p-values
  pvalue_data = pvalue_data,
  # column name containing adjusted p-values or raw p-values (p.value)
  p = "p.adj",
  # colors used for group visualization
  colors = c('#FFADAD', '#DEDAF4'),
  # selected feature/cluster ID for plotting
  cluster = 1948,
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out
)

5.5 Step 5: Beta diversity

Bray-Curtis dissimilarity compares sample abundance profiles, while PCoA displays their main differences. PERMANOVA tests group-associated variation in the full distance matrix; assess within-group dispersion when interpreting separation.

# The example uses group-selected significant_data; resulting group separation
# is exploratory.
# Use an unselected abundance table when testing an overall group-profile
# hypothesis.

# Perform beta diversity analysis and generate a PCoA plot
# `test` should be one of 'wilcox', 'ttest', 'kruskal', or 'anova'
MBR_beta(
  # dataframe containing features
  significant_data,
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out,
  # statistical test method
  test = 'wilcox',
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_name = 'Group',
  # colors used for group visualization
  colors = c('#FFADAD', '#DEDAF4')
)

5.6 Step 6: Feature selection

Recursive feature elimination compares predictor subsets through cross-validation. Importance scores and effect-size plots help explore selected features. Independent predictive evaluation requires feature selection inside an outer validation design.

# Choose rfe_size according to the number of available features.
# Cohen's d plots use log10(value + 1); effect estimates are exploratory after
# selection.

# Perform recursive feature elimination (RFE) for feature selection
# Random seeds are internally fixed for reproducibility.
MBR_fs(
  # dataframe containing features
  significant_data,
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out,
  # number of folds for cross-validation
  nfolds_cv = 5,
  # Largest requested subset size; caret also evaluates the full set.
  rfe_size = 199,
  # Number of selected features displayed in the importance plot.
  top_n_features = 10,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_name = 'Group',
  # metadata dataframe corresponding to samples
  meta_data = meta,
  # reference/control group used for comparison
  ref_group = 'CD',
  # colors used for visualization plots
  colors = c('#FFADAD', '#DEDAF4')
)

5.7 Step 7: SOM channel heatmap

Compare the scatter and fluorescence profiles represented by selected SOM nodes. pheatmap displays these channel patterns, with row scaling emphasizing relative values within each node.

# Plot all features retained by feature selection; the number can vary.
# Codebook row names must match feature identifiers; v/V prefix case is accepted.

# Generate a heatmap for selected features
MBR_heatmap(
  # selected feature matrix for visualization
  data = MBR_selected_features,
  # SOM prototype channel values
  cohonen_information = cohonen_information,
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out,
  # scaling method applied to rows
  scale = 'row',
  # whether to cluster columns
  cluster_cols = FALSE,
  # whether to cluster rows
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  # whether to display numeric values in the heatmap
  display_numbers = FALSE
)

5.8 Step 8: Metadata associations

A Mantel test compares sample-distance patterns, while the correlation heatmap summarizes relationships among microbial features. linkET combines these summaries in one display. Treat the associations as descriptive.

# Plot up to ten available selected features.
# Check that chosen metadata variables are numeric, finite and appropriately
# scaled.

# Perform Mantel correlation analysis between selected features and metadata
# variables
MBR_mantel(
  # selected feature matrix
  data = MBR_selected_features[, seq_len(min(10, ncol(MBR_selected_features))), drop = FALSE],
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta,
  # clinical variable columns
  clinical_cols = c("Clinical1", "Clinical2"),
  # demographic variable columns
  demographic_cols = c("Demographic1", "Demographic2"),
  # Assign readable labels to the metadata blocks.
  spec_select_names = list(
    # Label the clinical metadata block.
    A = "Clinical",
    # Label the demographic metadata block.
    B = "Demographic"
  # labels used for grouped variable categories
  ),
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out,
  # width of the output figure
  width = 6,
  # height of the output figure
  height = 6
)

5.9 Step 9: Random forest ROC diagnostic

The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve shows sensitivity across false-positive rates, and area under the curve (AUC) summarizes discrimination. See the pROC documentation for ROC estimation. This diagnostic uses held-out cross-validation probabilities averaged once per sample. Tuning and prior feature selection can still make the estimates optimistic; supply test_data and test_meta_data from unused samples for independent evaluation.

MBR_ml(
  # feature table
  data = MBR_selected_features,
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_name = 'Group',
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out,
  # reference group (e.g., "CD" or "HC")
  reference_level = 'CD',
  # width of the output plot PDF
  width = 6,
  # height of the output plot PDF
  height = 6,
  # resampling method
  method = 'repeatedcv',
  # number of folds
  number = 5,
  # number of repeats
  repeats = 2
)

5.10 Step 10: Confusion matrix

Inspect correctly classified samples and the types of classification error. The random forest confusion display uses held-out cross-validation predictions from a separately fitted model, or an independent test set supplied with test_data and test_meta_data. Group sizes matter when interpreting the counts.

# Generate a confusion matrix and classification performance summary
MBR_conf(
  # feature table used for model evaluation
  data = MBR_selected_features,
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_name = 'Group',
  # reference group (e.g., "CD" or "HC")
  reference_level = 'CD',
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = flow_out
)

5.11 Step 11: Reclustering

Group SOM prototypes into coarser signal profiles using standardized measurements and Ward hierarchical clustering. Cluster labels summarize similarity; they do not automatically update the mapped event assignments.

MBR_reclustering(data = cohonen_information, num_clusters = 1000)

5.12 Step 12: Flow cytometry channel plots

Locate selected SOM populations in scatter and fluorescence projections. The flowCore utilities read the mapped FCS files, while density backgrounds and prototype labels show where selected populations lie. Use transformations appropriate for the acquisition scale.

# file_index = 1 selects the first mapped FCS sample.
# Prototype row names must match selected_rows; annotation coordinates are
# aligned by cluster ID.

# Define the directory containing 'FCS files generated from SOM processing'
# Locate mapped FCS files produced by SOM analysis.
rawdata_path <- file.path(flow_out, "MappedFCS")

# Read the mapped FCS files into a flowSet.
fcs_files <- MBR_read(rawdata_path)

# Define selected SOM cluster IDs to visualize
# Choose the SOM cluster labels to inspect.
selected_rows <- c(
  'V1122','V1902','V1949','V978','V77','V1813','V1812','V1946','V205','V296'
)


# Define column name mappings between FCS channels and marker names
# Map acquisition-channel names to plotting labels.
column_mapping <- c(
  "FSC PAR"         = "FSC.PAR",
  "SSC"             = "SSC",
  "Hoechst.Red.DNA" = "Hoechst.Red",
  "Hoechst.Red"     = "Hoechst.Red",
  "Hoechst Red.DNA" = "Hoechst.Red",
  "FITC.hIgA2"      = "FITC",
  "FITC"            = "FITC",
  "APC.hIgA1"       = "APC",
  "APC"             = "APC",
  "Pe-TR.hIgG"      = "Pe.TR",
  "Pe.TR.hIgG"      = "Pe.TR",
  "Pe.TR"           = "Pe.TR",
  "BV650.hIgM"      = "BV650",
  "BV650"           = "BV650"
)

# Define marker/channel combinations for flow cytometry visualization
# Define the four scatter and fluorescence channel pairs.
plot_params <- list(
  list(x = "FSC.PAR", y = "SSC"),
  list(x = "FSC.PAR", y = "Hoechst.Red"),
  list(x = "FITC", y = "APC"),
  list(x = "Pe.TR", y = "BV650")
)

# Process a selected FCS file and apply signal transformation
# Prepare the selected FCS sample for channel plotting.
dat <- MBR_process(
  fcs_files,
  # Choose this position in the input FCS sample list.
  file_index = 1,
  # transformation function for scaling
  transformation = function(x) 10^((4 * x) / 65000),
  # defined channel mapping
  column_mapping = column_mapping
)

# Prepare SOM clusters for downstream visualization
# Prepare matching SOM prototypes for annotation.
bins <- MBR_prepare(
  cohonen_information,
  # selected SOM clusters
  selected_rows = selected_rows,
  # transformation function for scaling
  transformation = function(x) 10^((4 * x) / 65000),
  # defined channel mapping
  column_mapping = column_mapping
)

# Generate flow cytometry plots for selected channels and populations
# Create the arranged flow-density plots.
plots <- MBR_plot(
  # processed flow cytometry data
  dat = dat,
  # processed SOM cluster bins
  bins = bins,
  # marker/channel combinations for plotting
  plot_params = plot_params,
  # selected SOM clusters
  selected_rows = selected_rows
)

# Display generated plots
# Display the four-panel channel-density plot.
print(plots)

5.13 Step 13: Export selected populations

Save selected events for inspection in flow cytometry software. Export writes the supplied event values, so consider whether you want transformed or stored acquisition-scale values and retain channel names compatible with the source metadata.

# Use sample 1 consistently for processing and export metadata.
# Prepare acquisition-scale events with their original channel names.
export_dat <- MBR_process(fcs_files, file_index = 1, transformation = identity)

# Save selected gated populations/clusters as a new FCS file
MBR_save(
  # list of input FCS files
  fcs_files = fcs_files,
  # acquisition-scale events from the same source sample
  dat = export_dat,
  # selected clusters to export
  selected_rows = c("V9", "V10"),
  # Choose this position in the input FCS sample list.
  file_index = 1,
  # directory containing raw FCS files
  rawdata_path = rawdata_path
)

6 16S workflow (step 14)

This chunk runs when workflow is 16s or all. Its outputs use a separate folder.

6.1 Step 14: 16S rRNA gene sequencing

Compare 16S feature abundances between CD and HC and explore informative taxa with feature selection and classification. Ensure metadata matches the transposed sample order. This sample-level workflow is exploratory rather than a specialized sequencing count model.

# The feature table has taxa in rows and samples in columns.
# Use meta_final, matched to the transposed feature-table sample IDs.
# correction = "none" leaves p-values unadjusted.

# Pre-processing
# Load metadata and feature abundance table
# Read the matched 16S sample metadata.
meta_16s <- read.delim(
  # Read this file from the configured data folder.
  file.path(data_dir, "bac_meta.txt"),
  # Use the first file row as column headings.
  header = TRUE,
  # Use the first file column as row identifiers.
  row.names = 1
)
# Read the taxa-by-sample feature table.
count_table_16s <- read.delim(
  # Read this file from the configured data folder.
  file.path(data_dir, "bac_data.txt"),
  # Use the first file row as column headings.
  header = TRUE,
  # Use the first file column as row identifiers.
  row.names = 1
)

# This operation filters sample columns with zero totals, not taxon rows.
# Calculate totals for the sample columns of the imported 16S table.
col_sums <- colSums(count_table_16s)
# Retain sample columns with positive totals.
count_table_filtered <- count_table_16s[, col_sums > 0]

# Transpose the count table so that samples are rows and taxa are columns
# Transpose the feature table to samples in rows.
count_t <- as.data.frame(t(count_table_filtered))

# Reorder metadata to match the sample order in the feature table
# Reorder metadata rows to match the transposed sample identifiers.
meta_final <- meta_16s[rownames(count_t), , drop = FALSE]



# Application of MicroBiotR
MBR_stat(
  # feature abundance table
  data = count_t,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_col = 'Group',
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta_final,
  # statistical test method
  test_type = 'wilcox',
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = bac_out,
  # Set whether feature-wise p-values are adjusted for multiple tests.
  correction = 'none',
  # Set the feature-selection threshold for the chosen p-value column.
  cutoff = 0.1
)
## wilcox test
## Warning: Skipped 406 constant features with no variation; their p-values remain
## NA and they are excluded from significance selection.
##  DONE.
MBR_fs(
  # input dataframe containing significant features
  significant_data,
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = bac_out,
  # number of folds for cross-validation
  nfolds_cv = 5,
  # Largest requested subset size; caret also evaluates the full set.
  rfe_size = 125,
  # Number of selected features displayed in the importance plot.
  top_n_features = 10,
  # column name in metadata containing class/group labels
  group_name = 'Group',
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta_final,
  # reference/control group used for comparison
  ref_group = 'CD',
  # colors used for visualization plots
  colors = c('#FFADAD', '#DEDAF4')
)

7 RNA workflow (step 15)

This chunk runs when workflow is rna or all. Its outputs use a separate folder.

7.1 Step 15: Transcriptomics

Compare the supplied RNA expression profiles between HC and UC. Confirm expression units and normalization before interpreting gene-level differences, and ensure metadata follows sample order. A classifier evaluated on the same samples used for gene selection remains exploratory.

# Use meta_final, matched to the transposed expression-table sample IDs.
# correction = "none" leaves gene p-values unadjusted.
# reference_level identifies the positive class for ROC and confusion metrics.

# Pre-processing
# Load metadata and feature abundance table
# Read the RNA sample metadata.
meta_rna <- read.delim(
  # Read this file from the configured data folder.
  file.path(data_dir, "meta_rna.txt"),
  # Use the first file row as column headings.
  header = TRUE,
  # Use the first file column as row identifiers.
  row.names = 1
)
# Read the expression CSV with gene symbols and sample columns.
count_table_rna <- read_csv(
  # Read this file from the configured data folder.
  file.path(data_dir, "rnaibd.csv")
)

# Keep Symbol and numeric sample columns with positive totals.
# Retain Symbol and numeric columns with positive totals.
count_table_clean <- count_table_rna %>%
  # Select identifiers and the numeric columns described below.
  select(
    # Retain the gene identifier column.
    Symbol,
    # Keep numeric sample columns whose total is positive.
    where(~ is.numeric(.) && sum(., na.rm = TRUE) > 0)
  )

# Convert the `Symbol` column into row names so that genes become rows prior
# to transposition
# Use gene symbols as row identifiers before transposing.
count_df <- count_table_clean %>%
  # Convert the Symbol column into gene row names.
  column_to_rownames(var = "Symbol")

# Transpose the count table so that samples are rows and genes/features are
# columns
# Transpose the feature table to samples in rows.
count_t <- as.data.frame(t(count_df))

# Reorder metadata to match the sample order in the feature table
# Reorder metadata rows to match the transposed sample identifiers.
meta_final <- meta_rna[rownames(count_t), , drop = FALSE]



# Application of MicroBiotR
MBR_stat(
  # feature abundance table
  data = count_t,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_col = 'Group',
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta_final,
  # statistical test method
  test_type = 'wilcox',
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = rna_out,
  # Set whether feature-wise p-values are adjusted for multiple tests.
  correction = 'none',
  # Set the feature-selection threshold for the chosen p-value column.
  cutoff = 0.00001
)

MBR_ml(
  # feature table
  data = significant_data,
  # matched sample metadata data frame
  meta_data = meta_final,
  # column name in metadata containing group labels
  group_name = 'Group',
  # Write outputs to this workflow's output folder.
  out_path = rna_out,
  # reference group
  reference_level = 'UC',
  # width of the output plot PDF
  width = 6,
  # height of the output plot PDF
  height = 6,
  # resampling method
  method = 'repeatedcv',
  # number of folds
  number = 5,
  # number of repeats
  repeats = 2
)

The constant-feature summaries are expected on sparse 16S/RNA tables; their p-values stay NA. Installed linkET versions may emit ggplot2 deprecation warnings during the Mantel plot. They do not stop the example.
